messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The assault happened seven years ago, in the small, cluttered office of a man who had hired him as a part-time academic consultant. James, then fifty, had thought they were reviewing grant language. He remembered the hand on his shoulder, the shift in tone, the sudden, paralyzing grip. He remembered the smell of stale coffee and the sound of a wall clock ticking. What he could not remember, no matter how hard he tried, was the sequence of events that followed. His memory of the event was at once impossibly vivid and strangely incomplete. He could see the pattern of the man’s tie and the way the afternoon light fell across the desk, but there were minutes—whole stretches of time—that felt like a blank, a gap he could not fill. When he tried to tell his sister about it later, the words simply would not come; he knew what had happened, but his throat would close and his mind would go white, as if the language for it had been erased.

Afterward, James began to feel that his own body had betrayed him. He could no longer trust it to be strong or safe, and this sense of physical unreliability bled into a broader, constant vigilance. He had to be careful, he told himself, because you never knew what could happen next. This vigilance was not abstract. When a male student asked for a private tutoring session in a quiet corner of the library, James felt his chest tighten. The trigger—being alone with a man—immediately sharpened his threat monitoring. He would watch the student’s hands, the way he leaned in, scanning for any flicker of intention that might signal harm. The memory of the assault would then surface, unbidden, as if the trigger had unlocked a door. The vivid images—the tie, the light, the hand—would play behind his eyes, and with them came the crushing feeling of being set apart from others, isolated by something he could not explain. He had come to believe that other people lived in a world where bodies were trustworthy; he no longer lived there.

This constellation of negative appraisals—that he was alone, that his body was a liability, that danger was constant—drove his strategies. He began to avoid any situation that stirred strong emotions, because those emotions felt like a warning sign. He took up smoking, a habit he had quit decades earlier, because the ritual of it gave his hands something to do and his mind a narrow focus. Most of all, he avoided being touched. A hand on his arm from a well-meaning colleague would send a jolt through him, and he would pull away, apologizing, making excuses. The need to monitor for touch became exhausting. He started watching people closely for signs that they might harm him, reading their posture, their eye contact, their proximity. This threat monitoring, in turn, fed the memory. Every time he scanned a room for exits, every time he chose a seat with his back to a wall—a safe seat, he called it—the memory of the assault felt closer, more present, as if his vigilance kept it alive. The memory then reinforced his negative appraisals: see, you were right to be afraid, you were right to feel alone. He began to avoid unfamiliar places entirely because he could not assess the danger, and this avoidance meant he turned down tutoring jobs at new locations, shrinking his professional world.

The cycle tightened. His isolation deepened. He stopped going to a weekly book club he had enjoyed for years because the host, a man, had once clapped him on the back. The feeling of being forced to do something—even something as small as attending a party—became a trigger in itself, a loss of autonomy that echoed the original violation. The more he avoided, the more his negative appraisals seemed confirmed. He was isolated. He had to be careful. His body was not to be trusted. The memories, instead of fading, grew more intrusive, more vivid, and yet still incomplete, leaving him with the haunting sensation that the worst parts were hidden from him.

What finally brought James to seek help was not a crisis, but a quiet, cumulative despair. He was now fifty-seven, single, and tutoring only from his own apartment, with a strict policy that no male students could come inside. He had smoked his way up to a pack a day. He had not let anyone hug him in over a year. One evening, he realized he could not remember the last time he had felt anything other than watchful or afraid. He was tired of being set apart. He was terrified that this was all that was left. But he had also begun to wonder, for the first time, whether the gap in his memory might be a place he could finally look into, if he had someone to help him find the words.
